name: Tinder experiment

lead: A Tinder experiment is a test where a person (or a volunteer) uses a profile built around one person's photos, with a plain bio, in a set location, then records likes and matches over a few hours. Looksmaxxing forum users run them on models, influencers or their own pictures to see how different looks, photos or styling perform.

It helps looks work because it gives quick feedback on which photos, grooming or styling draw the most response. Results are anecdotal: forum threads post counts such as 51 likes and 6 matches in four hours for one model, and 3 likes and 2 matches for another.

paras: Typically a profile is created with a model's or user's photos, a generic bio and a set age and distance range, run for a few hours in one city, and screenshots of likes and matches are posted. Some threads ask for volunteers to use a user's photos on their own accounts.

Using someone else's photos can involve impersonation and can breach the platform's rules. Results vary with location, timing, photo choice and the app's algorithm, which commenters in these threads argue about.

angle.text: Experiments give people a quick, if informal, read on how their photos or looks are received, which they use to choose photos, grooming and styling. Forum members also use them to compare models and influencers.

lead: A Tinder experiment is a looksmaxxing practice in which a dating-app profile is run using one person's photos and a minimal bio, and the resulting likes and matches are used as a measure of how that appearance performs.[1][2][3] The practice is a staple of looksmax.org, where threads titled "Tinder experiment" post screenshots of likes and matches for models, influencers, YouTubers and forum members.[1][2][3][4][5]

Participants use the results to compare faces and photo sets, to test whether a change in photos, styling or grooming draws more response, and as informal evidence in arguments about how much looks matter in dating. Tinder, launched in 2012, is a swipe-based app in which two users must both like each other before they can message, and it relies far more on photos than earlier dating services did.[6]

The forum tests are single, uncontrolled trials. Separate published research has examined how dating-app users respond to profiles: a 2016 study of Tinder in London and New York used automated test accounts and found large differences in how often men and women were matched, and a 2025 experiment with 445 German app users found that photo attractiveness had the strongest influence on swiping decisions.[7][8]

paras: A Tinder experiment treats a dating app as a measuring instrument. A profile is built from one person's photos, given a deliberately ordinary bio and a set age range and search radius, and left running for a fixed period, usually a few hours. The poster then screenshots the likes and matches and shares them in a thread.[2][3] Some posters run several profiles at once in the same city, so that differences between them are attributed to the faces rather than to location or time of day.[2]

Threads on looksmax.org present results from profiles built around a model's or influencer's photos.[2][3] One user asked for volunteers to use his photos on their profiles to observe responses and matches.[1] Other threads titled as Tinder experiments cover YouTubers, models and requests for tests of particular people's photos, which shows how common the format became.[4][5][9][10]
Posters describe settings such as a 30 km radius in a large city and an age range, with a deliberately ordinary bio and an adjusted listed height.[3]

Tinder began as the prototype "Matchbox", presented by Sean Rad and engineer Joe Munoz on February 16, 2012, and was renamed Tinder before a soft launch on the iOS App Store in September 2012; an Android version followed in July 2013.[6] Users see a profile of photos, a short bio and interests, and swipe right to like or left to pass. Matching is double opt-in: individual choices stay hidden unless both people swipe right, and only then can they message.[6]

Wikipedia reports that Tinder weights photos much more heavily than earlier dating services, which matched mainly on biographical details, and quotes a 2014 New York Times article saying users read cues such as social status and confidence from the sequence of photos.[6] In the U.S. about 73% of users are men.[6]

Tinder was widely reported to keep a hidden internal ranking of users, often called an Elo score after the chess rating system. In March 2019 Tinder said in a blog post that it no longer used the Elo score to create matches, calling it an outdated measure, and that its newer system reorders the profiles a person sees as others like or pass on them.[11] Forum threads cite this kind of hidden ranking when posters argue about whether an account has been suppressed.[2]

In one thread a British model's profile got 51 likes and 6 matches in four hours, run at night in the same location as earlier tests. The poster presented it as a response to users who had attributed low results for another model to a shadowban or to detection of a fake profile.[2]

In another, a profile of a different model run in Cracow got 3 likes and 2 matches, which the poster described as a poor result. Replies suggested the photos looked too polished or that selfies had been used.[3] The same thread author also used the experiment to comment on the women he saw in the city, a pattern common in these posts, where the test doubles as an informal survey of the local pool.[3] Commenters in the threads attribute differences between profiles to photo style, location and timing rather than to the face alone.[2][3]

No formal study is tied to the forum practice, but several published projects used similar methods. In 2016 a team led by Gareth Tyson at Queen Mary University of London reported "A First Look at User Activity on Tinder". Because they could not access Tinder's own data, they created 14 fake accounts, mostly in London and some in New York, and used software to like profiles and log how often others responded, crawling roughly 230,000 male and 250,000 female profiles.[7]

They found that men liked most of the women they viewed but were matched only about 0.6% of the time, while women were far more selective and were matched about 10% of the time. About 86% of the matches received by male profiles came from men. For the male profiles, adding more photos or a written bio increased matches, and a bio raised average matches from women roughly fourfold.[7][6] The authors proposed a feedback loop in which low match rates push men to like more profiles while high match rates let women be more selective, and noted that only Tinder could confirm what happens at scale.[7]

A 2025 study by Jessika Witmer and colleagues at the University of Amsterdam, published in Computers in Human Behavior Reports, used conjoint analysis with 445 dating-app users in Germany, equally divided between men and women. Each participant judged 12 sets of fake profiles that varied attractiveness, height, job prestige, intelligence and bio quality, giving 5,340 decisions. Physical attractiveness was the strongest factor for both sexes; for average profiles, a one-standard-deviation improvement in photo attractiveness raised the matching rate from 25% to 43%, while the same improvement in the bio added about 2%. The profiles used AI-generated photos and the work measures initial attraction, not long-term compatibility.[8]

Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as having emerged from incel-era forums such as the PSL community, which rated men's faces on a numeric scale and sorted them into tiers, and later spread to TikTok.[12] In that setting Tinder experiments serve as a way to check ratings against real-world response, and posters sometimes frame a result as confirming or contradicting a model's reputation. The Cracow thread, for instance, reports a poor result for a prominent model and reacts by moving his photos into a different folder of the poster's reference images.[3]

Commenters regularly dispute what a result means. Replies in the threads point to natural versus polished photos, selfies versus professional shots, time of day and city as explanations, and some posters argue over shadowbans and fake-profile detection.[2][3] Beyond fixed experiments, users also post requests for others to test a specific person's pictures.[1][9]

Running a profile with another person's photos can amount to impersonation and may breach the platform's rules, and Tinder has publicly worked on verification features, including a "Verified Human" badge introduced in April 2026.[6] Results depend on location, time, photo selection and the app's ranking system, so threads caution each other about comparing results from different cities or hours.[2][3]
No studies found on the forum experiments themselves. Related published work on Tinder and attractiveness is described above.[7][8]

lore.intro: Forum users post experiment results as evidence about how much looks matter in dating and as a way to compare faces.[2][3]
